sentences.text: Betelgeuse shows what a star nearing the end of its life looks like.
When the hydrogen in its core ran out, it swelled into a red supergiant; if it were in the Sun's place, it would extend as far as Jupiter's orbit.
It is only 10 million years old, but because it is about 15 times as massive as the Sun, it used up its fuel very quickly.
In 2019 it suddenly dimmed; a giant dust cloud that broke away from its surface had veiled it.
Within the next 100,000 years it will explode as a supernova and be visible even in daylight.
Massive stars, on the other hand, die much more noisily.
The Crab Nebula is the remnant of a supernova recorded by Chinese and Arab astronomers in 1054.
That explosion was visible even in daylight for three weeks.
Today this filamentary cloud, 6 light-years across, continues to expand at 1,500 kilometers per second.
At its center is the neutron star left over from the explosion: the Crab Pulsar, spinning 30 times a second.
The iron, gold, and other heavy elements in the star are scattered into space by explosions like this; the calcium in your body was once inside a star.
And for the most massive stars, the final stop: a black hole.
Cygnus X-1 is the first black hole to be discovered.
This object of 21 solar masses draws gas from its blue supergiant companion; the gas heats to millions of degrees in the accretion disk and emits X-rays.
The two orbit their common center of mass once every 5. 5 days.
Not even light can escape from inside the event horizon.
A journey that begins in a gas cloud ends in a hole opened in spacetime itself.
The life of stars tour ends here.
On this tour we will follow the life story of a star, from its birth to its death.
The story begins in places like this: the Orion Nebula, a giant star factory 1,350 light-years away from us.
Cold gas and dust collapse under their own weight, forming hundreds of new stars.
The four bright Trapezium stars at the center illuminate the nebula from within with their ultraviolet light.
In the sky it is seen with the naked eye as the fuzzy patch in Orion's sword.
Stars are not born alone; they are born together with their siblings.
The Pleiades is a young family just like this.
It is about 100 million years old; compared with the Sun, it counts as a baby.
It contains more than 1,000 stars, but with the naked eye usually six or seven of them are seen; that is why, in many cultures, it is known as the Seven Sisters.
The haze around its bright blue stars is the reflection of a dust cloud that the cluster is passing through.
Within a few hundred million years these siblings will disperse and mix into the galaxy.
Medium-mass stars like the Sun do not explode; they gently blow their outer layers into space.
The Ring Nebula is the most beautiful example of this.
This colorful shell, 2,500 light-years away, is the outer layers cast off a few thousand years ago by a dying star.
The tiny white dot remaining at the center is its core, at a temperature of 120,000 degrees, and it makes the gas shine with its ultraviolet light.
In about 7 billion years the Sun, too, will become a planetary nebula like this.
Sirius is the brightest star in the sky; it is only 8. 6 light-years away from us.
But what really interests us is its small companion Sirius B, which remains in the shadow of its brightness.
This is a white dwarf: the core left behind by a dead star.
It has the mass of the Sun and the size of the Earth; a teaspoon of its matter weighs a ton.
It no longer produces energy, and only cools slowly over billions of years.
This is the Sun's ultimate fate as well.
The longest and calmest period of a star's life is the main-sequence phase.
The Sun is in exactly this phase: for 4. 5 billion years it has been converting hydrogen into helium in its core, and it will continue to do so for about 5 billion years more.
Every second it burns 600 million tons of hydrogen.
This delicate balance between the pressure pushing outward and the gravity pulling inward keeps the star stable.
When this balance breaks down, old age begins.
